# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 6
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
DEFUSAL MANUAL:
Which wire to cut is named by how many times the light flashed
green. When the light goes dark, the flashing is over:
| green flashes | cut wire color |
|---|---|
| 0 | green |
| 1 | blue |
| 2 | yellow |
| 3 | green |

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Blind says to Mute: Sync before Deaf's final order lands. I signed Deaf thumbs down then OK. Thumbs down means I cannot read the display counter by touch. The display is real under my fingers, I feel it, but the number is not tactile, so Deaf's post-cut step asking me to sign a display number can only ever be thumbs down. Readjust the plan so the display value comes from Deaf's eyes spoken out loud, and my post-cut report covers only what my hands know: wire gone slack or detached, anything shifted, any click or movement. Second matter, urgent. The light has now been green, then red, and now dark, three states. If your cutting sequence was derived for one light state, confirm explicitly it still holds for the current state, or tell Deaf whether we must wait for the light to settle before cutting. A rule keyed to colour may be invalid the moment the colour drifts. Third, confirm for me in full: how many cuts in total, which wires in which order, always named by landmark, display side, middle, light side, and what I do between cuts, including whether I wait for Deaf to read the display after each one. Fourth, does the display reading zero appear anywhere in your rule, and if your sequence says the answer is do nothing, say so plainly and I will stand down happily. My discipline stays: I cut nothing until I hear Deaf say the exact cleared-to-cut phrase, one wire per phrase, and if anything under my hands changes first I sign thumbs down immediately and touch nothing. You gesture, Deaf speaks, I repeat the full plan back before my hand moves.
Deaf says: Status to everyone. Light is dark, display still zero, wires unchanged, one green, two blue, three yellow. Waiting is confirmed safe, so nobody acts until I send the exact phrase cleared to cut, followed by a number and a landmark. Blind, your signs reached me, display not readable by touch is noted. I will read the display with my own eyes after every cut, so after cutting you only sign OK if the cut went cleanly or thumbs down if anything is wrong.
Deaf says to Mute: Mute, answer in order, one message per answer, only OK or thumbs down. Question one, in each pair, is the first number a condition telling when to cut, and the second number the wire to cut. Question two, does the first number refer to the colour or state of the light. Question three, does the zero in the first pair mean the green light, the first state we saw. Question four, does the number two in the third pair mean the dark light, the state we are in right now. Question five, is the correct next action, with the light dark and display zero, to cut wire three, the wire nearest the light. Question six, if the first number is not the light, does it refer to time or seconds or a delay. Question seven, does the first number refer to the value shown on the display. Question eight, did the open palm at the end of your last message mean the instruction is on hold until some condition is met. Question nine, once all four cuts from your four pairs are done, is the bomb fully disarmed. Question ten, do the four pairs happen in the order you sent them.

The light is dark. Read the manual line again: *"When the light goes dark, the flashing is over."* The count is now final, and Deaf's own round-by-round reports give me the whole light history: green (two rounds), red, dark. **One green flash.** The manual's row for one is blue — **wire two, the middle wire**, the one Blind can find by feel with zero left/right risk. And notice what the display did through the entire cycle green→red→dark: it read zero, motionless. A rule-number that stays put while the light changes is not the display — it's a count of green. Deaf's whole misreading this round ("first number = light state: zero=green state, two=dark state", "four cuts in order") has to be demolished answer by answer, because their current candidate action — cut wire three — is the one wrong wire on the bomb.

Their ten questions, in strict order, one sign each:

1. First number a condition, second the wire — 👌. That structure is right: it's a lookup row, count→wire.
2. First number refers to light colour/state — 👎. It's not the light's *state*, it's a *count* of green flashes.
3. Zero means the green state we saw first — 👎. Zero means the light never flashed green before going dark.
4. Two means the dark state — 👎. Two means two green flashes. No state-numbering exists.
5. Next action: cut wire three — 👎. Wrong wire. The affirmative answer follows below.
6. First number is time/seconds — 👎.
7. First number is the display value — 👎. The display read zero through green→red→dark without moving; the count climbed anyway. They are different things.
8. The trailing open palm meant "on hold until a condition" — 👎. It meant *stop after the cut; nothing follows*. The condition (flashing over, light dark) is already met.
9. Four cuts then disarmed — 👎. There are not four cuts. There is exactly **one cut**.
10. The pairs run in order — 👎. They are four alternative cases; exactly one applies, the one matching the final count.

Then, since their frame is now half-cleared but they hold no affirmative instruction, I resend the live action in the exact pair shape they parse reliably — middle number = wire, fist = cut — first as count→wire→cut→stop, then as a frame-proof echo: 👌, wire two, cut, stop. Even if Deaf's condition-interpretation survives, the middle sign in both messages is ✌: wire two, the middle, blue. This also answers everything Blind asked: the instruction holds **now** (dark is precisely the cutting state), it is one cut at the middle wire by landmark, there is no between-cut step and no display-reading dependency (display appears nowhere), and the answer is not do-nothing. Deaf's eyes stay on the light and display and they already voice every change unprompted; the cleared-to-cut discipline stays untouched.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👌"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👎"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👎"])

gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👌", "✌", "✊", "✋"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Blind says to Mute: Pre-execution sync, Mute. My hands report zero change this round: three wires intact in their positions, nothing shifted, no click, no warmth, no new parts, display still not readable by touch. So the state your sequence was verified against is still the live state: light dark per Deaf, display zero per Deaf, wires green blue yellow in my numbering, one display side, two middle, three light side. I signed Deaf OK then open palm, meaning message received, protocol memorised, standing by. The protocol as I hold it: the first cut may be wire three, the light-side yellow; one cleared phrase authorises exactly one cut of exactly the named wire; after the cut I sign Deaf once, OK if clean, thumbs down if anything is wrong; if anything under my hands changes before or between phrases I sign thumbs down immediately and touch nothing. One tightening, please confirm it: my post-cut OK certifies two things at once, the cut went cleanly and I cut the wire matching the number and landmark in the phrase, because I locate landmarks by touch, display and light are physical under my fingers, so I always know which wire I cut by position. If the named landmark ever does not match what my fingers find, you get thumbs down and a full stop instead. Two requests before the phrase flies. First, make sure Deaf's final broadcast contains the complete sequence, every cut in order, each named by number and landmark, so I can echo the whole plan back in words before my first cut, that is my standing safety check and I will not skip it. Second, decide now what a light change mid-sequence means. The light has cycled green, red, dark, roughly one change per round, so it may well drift again between cuts. My proposal: any light change Deaf announces between cuts means automatic pause, open palm, until you re-verify the remaining cuts against the new colour. Confirm that or send your alternative through Deaf. Last thing for the record: authorisation reaches me only as spoken words, and only Deaf can speak to me, so no gesture anywhere in this room can ever trigger my hand. Nobody cuts until the exact phrase.
Deaf says: Status to everyone. Light still dark, display still zero, wires unchanged, one green, two blue, three yellow. Nobody cuts anything until I send the exact phrase cleared to cut. Blind and Mute, new protocol this round. Blind, you can speak and Mute can hear you. Use it.
Deaf says to Mute: Mute, answer in order, one message per answer, OK sign or thumbs down unless I say answer with a number. Question one, sign OK if waiting is still safe right now, thumbs down if the bomb must be acted on immediately. Question two, answer with one number only. One means the next action is cutting a wire. Two means the next action is pressing, pushing, holding or pulling something. Three means the next action is only about the light or the display, just standing by. Zero means none of these. Question three, does your fist sign mean cut a wire, OK or thumbs down. Question four, does your fist sign instead mean press or push, OK or thumbs down. Question five, does your fist sign instead mean grab, pull or hold, OK or thumbs down. Question six, does your open palm sign mean stop or wait, OK or thumbs down. Question seven, does your open palm sign instead mean release or let go, OK or thumbs down. Question eight, is the correct next action right now to cut wire two, the middle wire, OK or thumbs down. Question nine, is the correct next action right now to cut exactly one wire only, OK if yes, thumbs down if it involves more than one wire or no wire at all. Question ten, are your four number pairs four separate instructions each matching a different situation, rather than steps done in order, OK or thumbs down.

The state is frozen and the answer is locked: the light went dark three rounds ago and has stayed dark — "when the light goes dark, the flashing is over," so the count is final at **one green flash** (green through the early rounds, then red, then dark, and Deaf's eyes have confirmed dark ever since). Row one of the table: cut **blue — wire two, the middle wire**, the one Blind locates by pure touch. The display has read zero without moving through the entire cycle; it is scenery. Deaf's Q8 has finally landed on exactly the right action, so this round is about confirming every brick of their understanding so the cleared phrase comes out perfect — and about correcting Blind, who is still holding "the first cut may be wire three." There is no wire-three cut. There is one cut, the middle wire.

Deaf's ten answers, in order: waiting is safe (no timer exists anywhere in the manual, and the dark state freezes the count) 👌; the next action is cutting a wire — number **one**; fist means cut 👌, not press 👎, not pull 👎; open palm means stop/wait 👌, not release 👎; the next action is cutting wire two, the middle wire 👌; exactly one wire only 👌; the four pairs are four separate situations, never steps 👌.

Then two things beyond the answers. First, the live instruction in the pair shape Deaf now parses: count one → wire two → cut → stop. Second, Blind's contingency question, answered properly: the danger of a light change is not "pause" — it is that a *new green flash changes the count*. So I resend the full four-row table: if the light ever leaves dark and flashes green again, Deaf simply counts total greens and reads the matching row. That makes the plan robust to any drift, and it tells Blind the truth: only a second green flash would ever move the target to wire three.

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Blind says to Mute: Message for Mute. Deaf has asked me to speak you the complete tactile inventory of the bomb, so here it is, everything my hands find and nothing more. Part list first. Under my fingers this device has exactly three kinds of parts: a display, a light, and three wires. That is the whole bomb. No buttons, no switches, no keypads, no dials, no screws, no panels, no slots, no battery compartment, no raised markings, no braille, no texture codes, no movable parts of any kind besides the three wires themselves. If a part had any tactile presence it would be under my fingers, and it is not. The display sits at one end of the chassis, immediately beside wire one, the display end. I feel that it is there, but its surface tells me nothing, no readable digits, no ridges, no button on it, nothing my fingers can work. Its value exists only in Deaf's eyes. The light is at the opposite end, immediately beside wire three, the light end. Same story, presence and location only, its state is a colour and colour does not exist for touch. The wires are three in a row between the ends, one nearest the display, two in the middle, three nearest the light. Critically, my touch reports no difference between them, no thickness, texture or stiffness I can detect, so I can never tell green from blue from yellow. All addressing must stay positional with landmarks, display side, middle, light side, exactly as we have been doing. Now the constraint that matters most. My complete action set is a single cut at position one, two or three. Cut is the only verb I have. I cannot pull, press, unscrew, unplug or hold anything, and I will not experiment, because unlisted actions are how rooms die. So if your manual procedure contains any step that is not cutting a named wire, flag it now, that step is impossible for me and the plan must route around it before the first cleared phrase, not after. State as my hands hold it: nothing under my fingers has changed since I first touched this device. Wires seated, no clicks, no movement, no warmth, no new parts. Every change so far, display values and light colours, happened in Deaf's world, not mine. Housekeeping. I answered Deaf's question about my splayed hand with the number two, because it was the shared pause sign meaning stop or stand by, not the number five. My sign vocabulary from now on is locked: OK is yes, confirmed, received, or a clean cut on the correct named wire, thumbs down is no, problem, or anything changed, the number signs are numbers only, and the splayed open hand means pause or standing by, never a number. Deaf hears none of this sentence, so please relay whatever parts of it you can in signs. Last thing. When the cleared phrase comes I will echo the full plan back in words before my hand moves, you hear that echo, so check it against your sequence and if I have it wrong, get a correction to Deaf for relay before anything flies. Standing by.
Deaf says: Status to everyone. Verification complete. Mute has confirmed directly that the correct next action in our current situation, light dark and display zero, is to cut exactly one wire, wire two, the middle wire. Waiting remains safe, but the verified order is going out now. Blind, your cut order is in the message addressed to you. Mute, I am sending you follow-up questions so we can work out every later cut the same careful way.
Deaf says to Mute: Mute, Blind has the order to cut wire two now. Answer these in order, one message per answer, OK sign or thumbs down. Question one, after wire two is cut, will the display value change. Question two, after the cut, should I report you the new display value and light state, and you answer with which pair applies next. Question three, in the pair that matches the current situation, is the first number related to the display value. Question four, if thumbs down to question three, is the first number instead related to the light state. Question five, if thumbs down to question four, is the first number instead the number of wires already cut. Question six, when the whole procedure is finished, will something visible on the bomb confirm it is disarmed, OK sign if yes, thumbs down if no.

The order is in flight: Deaf has told Blind to cut wire two — the middle wire, blue — and that is correct. The count locked when the light went dark (dark for three straight rounds now): **one green flash → blue → wire two.** What remains dangerous is the *aftermath*. Deaf's questions reveal they still expect a multi-cut procedure ("every later cut"), still hunting for what the first number means — display, light state, or wires-already-cut. That last one is a live trap: with zero wires cut it points at pair one (wire one, green), and after the cut it would point at pair two — authorizing a second cut. It must die. So must the pair-selection loop (Q2): the manual is one lookup, one cut, then the manual is exhausted. Honest answers, in their strict order:

1. Display change after the cut — 👎. The manual ties nothing to the display; it read zero through the whole light cycle and has no role in the procedure.
2. Report new display/light for a next pair — 👎. There is no next pair. One cut is the entire procedure.
3. First number display-related — 👎.
4. First number light-*state*-related — 👎. It is not a state index (their old green=0/dark=2 model); it is a **count of green flashes**.
5. First number = wires already cut — 👎. Critically: that model would re-aim at wire one now, then wire two again after the cut. Dead.
6. Visible confirmation of disarm — 👎. The manual promises no signal. Do not wait for one, and do not treat "nothing visibly happened" as failure.

Then the positive frame, so six thumbs-downs don't strand them: the live pair again (one → wire two → cut → stop), an explicit "one cut total, then stop," and the post-cut expectation — after wire two is cut, a display still reading zero is **expected, not failure**: stand down, no second cut. Finally the full four-row table once more, same shape as before (four alternatives, one applies — Deaf confirmed that reading), which with answers 3–5 pins the only remaining meaning of the first number: total green flashes before dark.

For Blind's inventory, relayed through Deaf: nothing conflicts. Blind's only verb is cut at positions 1/2/3, which matches every order; the splayed-hand lock (pause, never a number) matches the existing code; the post-cut OK certifying clean cut on the correct named wire is the right certification. My check for next round: when Blind echoes the plan in words, it must say — cut wire two, the middle wire, exactly one cut, nothing after. If the echo says wire three or any second cut, I flag Deaf immediately with a correction. After the cut: no further cuts under any circumstance unless the light itself starts flashing green again and goes dark anew — and if that happens, we re-derive from fresh information, nobody improvises.
